# Spring Boot Web Application using Multi-Architecture Image Builds

This runbook uses the same Spring Boot quote application as the other Spring
Boot examples, but the focus is the container image metadata rather than the
application code. A multi-architecture image is not one image containing
portable native machine code. It is an OCI image index, also called a manifest
list, that points to one image manifest per target platform.

The goal is to make the platform boundary visible:

- a normal local image build produces one platform-specific image;
- a multi-platform build produces an image index with separate manifests;
- each platform variant must use runtime artefacts that are valid for that
  platform;
- `jlink`, CDS archives, and Leyden AOT caches are not portable across
  operating systems and CPU architectures.

This example deliberately uses a plain executable Spring Boot JAR. The JAR
contains architecture-neutral bytecode, while the Java runtime comes from the
selected platform variant of the base image. That keeps the first
multi-architecture lesson focused on image selection. If a Dockerfile creates a
custom runtime with `jlink`, generates a CDS archive, or records a Leyden AOT
cache, that work needs to happen separately for each target platform because
those outputs are tied to the operating system, CPU architecture, and runtime
build that produced them.

This is a focused example, not a complete Java-in-containers reference
architecture. It covers building and inspecting a multi-architecture container
image for a Spring Boot application, and deliberately leaves out concerns such
as non-root runtime users, image signing, vulnerability scanning, observability,
SBOM generation, layer optimisation, JVM ergonomics, and deployment-specific
hardening. Keeping those concerns out of this runbook makes the image index and
platform-specific manifest behaviour easier to reason about. For a more holistic
Spring Boot container example that combines several workshop concerns, see
[all-in-one-spring-boot](../all-in-one-spring-boot/README.md).

**Resources**

- [OCI Image Index Specification](https://github.com/opencontainers/image-spec/blob/main/image-index.md)
- [Docker Buildx](https://docs.docker.com/buildx/working-with-buildx/)
- [Docker multi-platform builds](https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-platform/)
- [Podman](https://podman.io/)
- [Skopeo](https://github.com/containers/skopeo)
- [Oracle Container Registry](https://container-registry.oracle.com/)

## Prerequisites

- [Oracle Java 25](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/downloads/#java25)

- Either [Docker](https://docs.docker.com/get-docker/) with Buildx, or
  [Podman](https://podman.io/) with manifest support.

- [Skopeo](https://github.com/containers/skopeo).

- `jq`, used to inspect OCI JSON documents.

Additional setup inputs:

- [Oracle Account](https://profile.oracle.com/myprofile/account/create-account.jspx)
  to access [Oracle Container Registry](https://container-registry.oracle.com/)

- An Oracle Container Registry authentication token stored in
  `~/.ocr/auth-token`, or an equivalent secure way to pass the password to
  the container tool through standard input.

- A container registry namespace if you want to push a runnable multi-platform
  tag. The main flow writes an OCI archive locally, so a registry is not
  required for the core inspection steps.

### Accept the Terms and Conditions

Before you can use the Oracle Java images, you need to accept the terms and
conditions by navigating to
[https://container-registry.oracle.com/ords/ocr/ba/java/jdk](https://container-registry.oracle.com/ords/ocr/ba/java/jdk)
and logging in.

1. Accept the
   [Oracle Container Registry](https://container-registry.oracle.com/) terms and
   conditions.

2. Log in to `container-registry.oracle.com` using your Oracle account.

   The container tool needs access to Oracle Container Registry before it can
   pull the Oracle Java base image referenced by the Dockerfile. This example
   reads an Oracle authentication token from `~/.ocr/auth-token` and passes it
   to the login command through standard input so the token is not written into
   the shell history. If you are using Podman instead of Docker, use the same
   registry, username, and token with `podman login --password-stdin`.

   ```shell
   docker login container-registry.oracle.com \
     --username 'ALBERT.ATTARD@ORACLE.COM' \
     --password-stdin < ~/.ocr/auth-token
   ```

   This should print the login succeeded message.

   ```
   Login Succeeded!
   ```

## Build the application

The application is built once. The resulting Spring Boot JAR is copied into each
platform-specific image. That separation matters: the Java bytecode is shared,
while the operating-system and CPU-specific runtime comes from the platform
variant of the base image.

1. Build the application.

   ```shell
   ./mvnw clean package
   ```

   (*Optional*) Verify that the application was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name -L 1 --prune './target/'
   ```

   Spring Boot creates one executable JAR containing the application classes,
   Spring Boot launcher, and nested dependency JARs.

   ```
   ./target/
   ├── multi-architecture-image-builds-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar
   └── multi-architecture-image-builds-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar.original

   1 directory, 2 files
   ```

2. Run the executable JAR as a baseline.

   This confirms that the packaged JAR works before the container steps add
   Dockerfiles and image layers to the picture.

   The application is started in the background for convenience, otherwise the
   subsequent commands need to be executed in another terminal.

   ```shell
   java -jar './target/multi-architecture-image-builds-spring-boot-1.0.0.jar' > './target/output.txt' 2>&1 &
   echo $! > './target/application.pid'
   ```

   Wait for the application to start.

   ```shell
   while [ "$(curl --silent --output /dev/null --write-out '%{http_code}' 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random')" -ne '200' ]
   do
     echo 'Waiting for the application to start'
     sleep 1
   done
   ```

   (*Optional*) Fetch a random quote.

   ```shell
   curl --silent 'http://localhost:8080/quote/random' | jq
   ```

   The response should be similar to the following.

   ```json
   {
     "author": "René Descartes",
     "id": 140,
     "quote": "I think therefore I am."
   }
   ```

3. Stop the application.

   ```shell
   kill "$(cat './target/application.pid')"
   ```

## Inspect the base image platforms

A multi-platform application image can only target platforms that are supported
by its base image. If the base image does not publish a variant for a requested
platform, the application image cannot produce a valid variant for that platform
without changing the base image.

1. Inspect the Oracle Java base image before building the application image.

   ```shell
   skopeo inspect --raw 'docker://container-registry.oracle.com/java/jdk:25.0.4.1' | jq
   ```

   The base image tag resolves to platform-specific image manifests.

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 2,
     "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.list.v2+json",
     "manifests": [
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
         "size": 1099,
         "digest": "sha256:06d115c14b85dc23030635780c6a587096dfb0583085c31d36be634b7efe49f2",
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "arm64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       },
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.docker.distribution.manifest.v2+json",
         "size": 1099,
         "digest": "sha256:c2fde8cea2f620b6b7dafc53fa9a4ac3f88ed41ad1ad35e085c56decdfc96d12",
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "amd64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   The Oracle Java base image used here publishes both `linux/arm64` and
   `linux/amd64` variants. Those are the two platforms requested later in this
   runbook.

## Build a local single-platform image

A normal local build creates one image for the builder’s default platform. That
is fine for local testing, but it does not create a multi-platform tag or an
image index. This is the behaviour many engineers see first: the image works on
the machine that built it, but it says nothing about other CPU architectures.

1. Build the container image for a single platform.

   ```shell
   docker build \
     --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
     --tag 'demo:multi-architecture-image-builds-local' \
     .
   ```

2. Inspect the local image platform.

   ```shell
   docker image inspect 'demo:multi-architecture-image-builds-local' \
     --format '{{.Os}}/{{.Architecture}}'
   ```

   A locally loaded image has one operating system and architecture.

   ```
   linux/amd64
   ```

## Build a multi-platform OCI archive

Docker Buildx and Podman can both produce a multi-platform OCI archive without
pushing to a registry. This is useful for workshop inspection because the output
is a normal tar file containing an OCI layout and image index. In a delivery
pipeline, the same idea usually ends with a push to a registry rather than a
local archive.

The Dockerfile copies an existing JAR and does not run target-architecture
binaries during the build. If the Dockerfile used `RUN jlink`,
`RUN java -Xshare:dump`, or a Leyden training run, the build would need
platform-aware execution for each target. Otherwise, an `amd64` build could
accidentally produce runtime artefacts that an `arm64` image cannot use, or the
other way round.

The Docker and Podman commands are both shown for completeness. Execute the
option that matches the environment used for the workshop.

1. Build the multi-platform OCI archive.

   The `--platform` option tells the builder which operating system and CPU
   architecture combinations to build for. Here we request two Linux image
   variants: `linux/amd64` for x86-64 machines and `linux/arm64` for 64-bit ARM
   machines. The resulting image reference can then point to both variants
   through a manifest list, allowing the container runtime to pull the matching
   image for the host platform.

   - Using Docker.

     ```shell
     docker buildx build \
       --platform 'linux/amd64,linux/arm64' \
       --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
       --tag 'demo:multi-architecture-image-builds-oci' \
       --output 'type=oci,dest=./target/multi-architecture-image-builds.tar' \
       .
     ```

     The `--output 'type=oci,dest=./target/multi-architecture-image-builds.tar'`
     option exports the build result as an OCI image archive instead of loading
     it directly into the local image store. The `dest` value specifies the tar
     file to create. Because this build targets multiple platforms, the archive
     contains an OCI image index together with the platform-specific image
     manifests and layers. This makes the archive useful for inspection,
     transfer, or later loading with tools that understand OCI archives, without
     requiring the image to be pushed to a registry first.

   - Using Podman.

     ```shell
     podman manifest rm 'demo:multi-architecture-image-builds-oci' 2>/dev/null || true

     podman build \
       --platform 'linux/amd64,linux/arm64' \
       --file './containers/Dockerfile' \
       --manifest 'demo:multi-architecture-image-builds-oci' \
       .

     podman manifest push \
       'demo:multi-architecture-image-builds-oci' \
       'oci-archive:./target/multi-architecture-image-builds.tar'
     ```

     `--manifest` names the Podman manifest list that collects the `linux/amd64`
     and `linux/arm64` images produced by this build. The subsequent
     `podman manifest push` command exports that manifest list, together with
     its platform-specific images, to the OCI archive.

   (*Optional*) Verify that the file was created.

   ```shell
   tree --dirsfirst --sort=name --prune -P '*.tar' './target'
   ```

   The OCI image archive should now be present under `target`.

   ```
   ./target
   └── multi-architecture-image-builds.tar

   1 directory, 1 file
   ```

2. Inspect the OCI image index stored in the archive.

   ```shell
   IMAGE_INDEX_DIGEST="$(
     tar --extract --to-stdout --file './target/multi-architecture-image-builds.tar' 'index.json' \
       | jq --raw-output '.manifests[0].digest | sub("^sha256:"; "")'
   )"

   tar --extract --to-stdout --file './target/multi-architecture-image-builds.tar' "blobs/sha256/${IMAGE_INDEX_DIGEST}" | jq
   ```

   The archive contains one image manifest per requested platform.

   ```json
   {
     "schemaVersion": 2,
     "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json",
     "manifests": [
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
         "digest": "sha256:2f57843f9d3211b0dafb5edd7caf790ba0da65f358554373e562af4f92632066",
         "size": 1325,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "arm64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       },
       {
         "mediaType": "application/vnd.oci.image.manifest.v1+json",
         "digest": "sha256:fd011b22c81dbdddc1390fa6edc4c96849c19231f6a3b55509cb62f8fd4e89a2",
         "size": 1325,
         "platform": {
           "architecture": "amd64",
           "os": "linux"
         }
       }
     ]
   }
   ```

   The command displays the archive’s OCI image index. Its `manifests` array
   contains one descriptor for each requested platform, identifying the
   platform-specific image manifest by digest. When the archive is published to
   a registry, a container runtime uses this index to select the manifest that
   matches the target platform.
